competitors.title: Ory Agent Security: See and control what your AI agents do
key_points: AI coding agents (Claude Code, Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw) spread in months, not years — they read/write source code, run shell commands, call internal APIs with developer credentials
Security and platform teams rarely approved agent adoption; most orgs can't count how many agents are running
Every other teammate has identity, permission scope, and audit trail — agents don't. Ory Agent Security closes that gap

Three pillars: Authenticated (who is acting — agent gets its own identity, distinct from human), Authorized (what can they touch — Keto policy engine checks every action), Accountable (what did they do — structured audit events to SIEM/Splunk/Datadog)
Starts in monitoring mode (observe without blocking), flips to enforcement mode when ready
Covers Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenCode, OpenClaw — spanning Anthropic, OpenAI, Google, and open source
Built on existing Ory stack (Kratos, Hydra, Keto, Oathkeeper) — no parallel system for existing customers

competitors.title: Ory Agent Security, the Security Plane for AI Coding Agents
key_points: In-the-loop enforcement built directly into the agent runtime — not a sidecar or gateway
Every agent and sub-agent authenticates with its own credentials before acting; delegation chain back to user is recorded
Fine-grained authorization on shell commands, file writes, MCP tools, server connections, and downstream API calls using Zanzibar-style permission model (Ory Keto)
Allowed, denied, escalated, and approved actions recorded via OpenTelemetry; delegation chain survives token expiry

Free plugins on Anthropic marketplace; npm packages for Claude Code, Gemini CLI, OpenAI Codex, OpenClaw, OpenCode

competitors.title: Ory Agent Security hands AI agents their own identity layer
key_points: Agents don't fit OIDC/OAuth2's three-role model (resource owner, client, authorization server) — agents are delegates acting on behalf of users with scoped authority
Token exchange via RFC 8693: user grants agent scopes, Ory issues short-lived access token with 'act' (actor) claim showing both user and agent
Policy engine via Keto evaluates relationship tuples in O(1) per check — critical when agents make hundreds of decisions per minute
Token mediation through Oathkeeper reverse proxy — opt-in per route, introspects token, enforces policy, rewrites claims
Comparison: Auth0 has token exchange but no first-class 'agent' entity; Okta has stronger SSO but needs extension for delegation; AWS Cognito + IAM Roles Anywhere is DIY audit story
Ory's edge: open-source stack built around Zanzibar-style relationship-based access control — maps cleanly to 'user authorizes agent to do X on resource Y'
Pushback: 'control plane' is ambitious for a new product; agent identity lacks standards (no OIDC-equivalent for agents); audit correlation with downstream actions is still the user's problem

angles: The governance gap: AI coding agents operate with developer credentials but no separate identity — Ory Agent Security gives agents their own identity, permission scope, and audit trail
Three pillars framework: Authenticated (who is acting), Authorized (what can they touch), Accountable (what did they do) — maps directly to CISO's three questions
Observe-before-enforce: Ory starts in monitoring mode so teams can see what would be blocked without interrupting developers, then flips to enforcement when ready
Agent DX vs Agent Security: two products for two lifecycle stages — DX for building auth into apps with AI agents, Security for governing agents in production

MCP security: Ory adds OAuth 2.1 authorization for MCP servers, solving the 'agent can call any MCP tool' problem with server-level and tool-level checks

outline: Introduction: The AI coding agent governance gap — agents running with developer credentials, no separate identity, no audit trail
The Problem: Why existing IAM (OIDC/OAuth2) doesn't fit agents — agents are delegates, not users; they need their own identity, scoped authority, and delegation chains
Ory Agent Security Overview: Three pillars — Authenticated, Authorized, Accountable — built on existing Ory stack (Kratos, Hydra, Keto, Oathkeeper)
Pillar 1 — Authenticated: Agent identity registration, distinct from human identity, delegation chain recording, sub-agent identities for background tasks
Pillar 2 — Authorized: Fine-grained authorization via Ory Keto (Zanzibar-style), policy evaluation per action, MCP server authorization with OAuth 2.1
Pillar 3 — Accountable: Structured audit events via OpenTelemetry, SIEM integration, delegation chain surviving token expiry
Observe-Before-Enforce: Monitoring mode to see what would be blocked, then flip to enforcement when policies are tuned
Agent DX vs Agent Security: Two products for two lifecycle stages — DX for building auth into apps, Security for governing agents in production
Supported Agent Harnesses: Claude Code, OpenAI Codex, Gemini CLI, OpenClaw, OpenCode — npm packages and marketplace plugins
Integration Walkthrough: Install plugin, define agent types, call token-exchange at task start, pass scoped tokens to tool-call layer

Comparison with Alternatives: Auth0, Okta, AWS Cognito, DIY — where Ory wins (Zanzibar model, open source, delegation out of the box) and where incumbents still lead (enterprise SSO, admin UI maturity)
Limitations and Risks: New product, no agent identity standards, audit correlation still user's responsibility, pricing unknown for scale
Future Outlook: Agent identity as a market segment, standards evolution, Ory's open-source bet vs incumbent catch-up
Conclusion: Why every engineering org with AI coding agents needs an agent IAM strategy — and how to start with Ory's free plugins
